name: Mock Trial
summary: Teams play the attorneys and witnesses in a made-up court case, from opening statements to closing arguments.
who: High school and college students on teams that prepare both sides of one case for the season.
team: Teams of about 6 to 12; each side has two or three attorneys and two or three witnesses
length: A trial takes about two to three hours
resolution: A case packet released before the season: the charges or claims, witness statements, exhibits and rules.
rewards: Careful reading of the case packet
Knowing the rules of evidence and making objections
Convincing openings and closings, and believable witnesses
start: Ask your state's bar association about its high school competition; many supply the case, rules and volunteer attorney coaches.
Read the case packet twice, once for each side.
Practice a short direct examination with open questions and a cross-examination with leading questions.
varies: High school competitions are run state by state, usually by bar associations, each with its own case and rules. College mock trial uses one case and rule set for all schools.

p: Debaters argue a resolution; mock trial teams argue facts in a case, inside courtroom rules. The skills overlap: cross-examination in mock trial is a close cousin of cross-ex in debate (short questions, one fact at a time), and openings and closings are persuasive speeches.
State winners in high school can go on to the National High School Mock Trial Championship, held since 1984. College teams compete through the American Mock Trial Association, founded in 1985.
